# Hand Grinder

## Overview

The tool I keep for travel is a conical steel set in an aluminium body, about 600 g, with a folding crank that tucks into the top of the catch cup. I take it camping and to rented flats where the countertop box would be too much to carry. It is slower than a motor, roughly ninety seconds for a single dose, and that is the trade for not depending on a socket. The catch cup threads on and off with a quarter turn, and the whole thing packs into a cloth bag about the size of a mug. I have had it for six years and it has never needed more than a brush and a clean.

## Setup

I set the zero point once, at the start, by turning the adjuster in until the burrs close and marking that collar position with a scratch of nail varnish. From that mark the numbers run coarse as they rise. Pour over sits at eighteen clicks, the stovetop pot at twelve, and a moka pot somewhere between. I weigh beans before they go in, twelve grams for one cup and twenty for the pot, because the adjustment moves with the load and the dose. The handle screw gets a quarter turn with a coin when the crank starts to feel slack. The burr carrier lifts out for cleaning, and the axle has two sealed bearings pressed into the body that I have never needed to replace.

To get the setting repeatable I always return the collar to the marked zero and count up from there, rather than trusting the numbers printed on the ring. The ring itself is only a guide: mine has drifted half a click clockwise over the years as the thread bedded in, which is why the varnish mark matters more than the digits. I keep a small card in the bag with my settings for the pot, the cone and the press, because after a few months away I forget which number was which. Water goes in at about ninety-four degrees for the cone, and I let the kettle sit for thirty seconds off the boil before I pour.

Air travel is the one thing that catches people out. The burr carrier sits loose in the body, so I take the crank off and pack the whole thing upright in the middle of the bag, wrapped in a shirt, with the collar tightened down past zero so nothing spins on the way. A carrier that has been rattling against the ring for a long flight arrives with its threads slightly flattened and the burr face scuffed, which is not fatal but does show up as a coarser first cup.

## Troubleshooting

The complaint I hear most from other owners is that the shaft has play. If the axle bearing has worn, the shaft rocks in the body and the burr face chews unevenly, so the cup pulls fast at one notch and slow at the next. Press the crank to the side with light finger pressure while it turns: a millimetre of movement at the burr is enough to explain a cup that changes character from morning to morning. A worn bearing is a workshop job, unless the body takes a pressed replacement, which mine does.

A graunchy, gritty feel through the crank is usually old grounds packed behind the carrier rather than a damaged burr face. Strip the body, brush the threads, and the sound goes. If the feel is still rough after that, look for a chipped tooth on the inner cone with a torch; a chipped cone cuts a mix of two sizes and no setting will fix it.

A crank that swings loose or drops under its own weight is a slack handle screw, or in bad cases a stripped thread in the knob. Tighten the screw first and only replace the knob if the thread has gone. A catch cup that unscrews while the crank turns means the cup threads want a wipe of dry wax, not oil, since oil collects dust and makes the problem worse.

The setting wandering after the tool has been knocked about is almost always the zero ring having been nudged, not the burr face wearing. Re-check the varnish mark before you adjust anything else, because chasing a setting from a moved reference will have you three clicks out and blaming the beans. Finally, a cup that tastes thin with a short contact time in the cone points at an uneven bed, so level the grounds with a tap before the water goes on.

## Notes

Brush it out every few days, never wash the body or the burrs in water, and keep the threads dry. A drop of dry lubricant on the axle once a year is plenty. The cloth bag matters more than it sounds: aluminium knocks against keys and cutlery and the anodising does not survive it. If the crank starts to squeak, that is the pivot, not the burrs, and a touch of grease on the pin quietens it for months. I keep a spare handle screw in the bottom of the bag, because a lost screw on a trip means brewing with a pair of pliers.
